summary: Redwood AE+SE walked NimbusPay through Redwood Optimize recommendations for batching and prefix/KV caching to reduce token costs while meeting latency SLOs. Discussed hit-rate assumptions, batching windows, cache sizing and TTL, quantization tradeoffs, and pilot benchmark plan. Customer raised PII/data residency and p99 latency concerns for payments flows. Agreed on delivering cost-model workbook, SOC2/network diagrams, and running a benchmark using customer traces.
topics: Prefix vs KV cache tradeoffs and sizing
Pilot / benchmark plan and next steps
transcript:
[00:00] Elena: Hey everyone thanks for carving time, um this is Elena from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. With me is Ravi, our solutions engineer. Hey Ravi.
[00:08] Ravi: Hi all, glad to be here. We'll run through Optimize — batching, the prefix/KV cache, cost model examples, and then leave time for questions.
[00:17] Markus: Thanks Elena, appreciate it. Quick note, we're super time boxed, we've got 55 minutes but prefer under an hour.
[00:23] Elena: totally, we'll keep it tight. Aisha, Tom — do you want to say quick roles?
[00:28] Aisha: Aisha, SRE, do infra + security for the ML workloads.
[00:31] Tom: Tom, product, owns the payments UX that will call the LLM.
[00:34] Markus: Markus, head of ML, overseeing model selection and perf.
[00:37] Elena: Great. We'll start with 1) quick context / goals, 2) batching basics and windows, 3) prefix vs KV cache, hit-rate assumptions and sizing, 4) cost model walkthrough, 5) pilot plan.
[00:48] Elena: Markus mentioned you have a latency SLO for payment intents?
[00:51] Markus: yeah target is p50 < 60ms, p99 < 450ms for the confirmation flow. It's not for every request — higher priority traffic — but we need predictability.
[01:02] Elena: good, that's in line with a lot of finance customers. Aisha, any constraints on network / VPC?
[01:07] Aisha: we need VPC peering or private link, can't have data egress to public. Also need KMS integration for keys and audit logs retention for 1 year.
[01:16] Ravi: that's fine, Redwood Private supports customer-managed VPC and KMS; we'll attach SOC2 artifacts in the doc pack.
[01:22] Tom: Cost is big too. Right now inference is eating into infra — curious how much KV/prefix cache helps.
[01:29] Ravi: great — we'll show a back-of-envelope and a workbook. First, quick batching primer.
[01:34] Ravi: We balance latency vs per-token cost by adjusting batching windows and queue size. If you batch aggressively you amortize model GPU setup cost across more tokens, lower cost per token, but higher latency.
[01:45] [01:47] Markus: what's a typical batching window you'd recommend for interactive UX?
[01:50] Ravi: for interactive text gen we suggest 10-30ms micro-batching plus dynamic batching for the rest; end-to-end you can keep p50 low. With Redwood pipeline we also do continuous batching while respecting per-request latency SLOs.
[02:03] Aisha: micro-batching 10-30ms seems tiny — does that still help cost materially?
[02:09] Ravi: yes at scale. Example: without any batching each request pays full kernel launch and KV management; with micro-batching + pooling you can reduce total GPU time by 15-30% for conversational workloads.
[02:20] Elena: we'll show a numeric example in the cost model.
[02:24] Ravi: now KV / prefix cache — short version: prefix cache caches key/value KV cache for recent prompts; prefix cache is for identical or near-identical prefixes (like template prompts) and KV caching stores computed key/value for attention to avoid recomputing for repeated prefixes.
[02:40] Tom: sorry is prefix cache same as session cache?
[02:42] Ravi: similar concept; prefix = the beginning tokens of a conversation or template. Session cache is session-specific; prefix cache is template-specific and can be shared across sessions. There can be overlap.
[02:52] Markus: what's realistic hit-rate we can expect for our payment confirmation prompts? We have a lot of templated language.
[02:58] Ravi: templated flows often see high prefix hit-rates — 40-70% depending on how many unique templates and whether you include user-specific variables. If your templates are stable and you strip variable tokens from cache keys you can boost hit-rate.
[03:11] Aisha: stripping variables — that's interesting, does Redwood provide tooling to normalize prompts?
[03:15] Ravi: yes we have a prompt normalization layer and examples in the workbook; common approach is replace PII placeholders before keying cache.
[03:23] Markus: what about TTLs and memory sizing?
[03:26] Ravi: TTL depends on traffic; for high QPS templates you can keep shorter TTL and still get high hit-rate. Memory sizing: we estimate average KV entry at ~1.2KB with metadata; for 1M entries that's ~1.2GB. In the workbook we'll show sizing curves.
[03:39] [03:40] Tom: any security concerns — are cached items stored encrypted?
[03:43] Elena: yes encryption at rest and customer KMS support; we can configure encryption keys per tenant in Private deployments.
[03:49] Ravi: sliding into cost models — I have a simple example: assume baseline model cost per GPU-hour and tokens/sec throughput. If you can get a 50% prefix hit-rate and 20-30% batching efficiency, your effective cost per generated token can drop by ~35-50% depending on model and quantization.
[04:09] Markus: can you show numbers please?
[04:12] Ravi: sure — open link (we shared cost-model.xlsx in chat). Quick example: 1M monthly gen tokens, 100k embeddings, using a 7B quantized profile. Baseline hosted run cost X (we'll put explicit numbers in workbook) — with 50% prefix hits -> you skip half of the decode compute for those requests. Add batching -> fewer launches -> lower p95 GPU utilization spikes. Net cost decrease in example: from $1,200/month -> $650-750/month.
[04:45] Aisha: that seems big, is it realistic?
[04:47] Ravi: depends on workload shape. If you have many unique prompts with low template reuse then hit-rate will be lower. Workbook has sensitivity table for hit-rate 10/30/50/70%.
[04:58] Elena: also note model choice matters — smaller quantized models amplify benefit of caching but you need to validate quality.
[05:05] Markus: what about p99 latency — does caching hurt or help?
[05:09] Ravi: caching helps p99 for cache-hit traffic because you avoid recompute; however, if cache-miss traffic batches and triggers heavier load you can see p99 spikes. That's why Redwood routing gives priority queues and fallback models to maintain p99 SLOs.
[05:22] Tom: fallback models?
[05:24] Ravi: e.g., route urgent traffic to a smaller but faster model variant pinned to dedicated pool; lower priority traffic goes to cheaper shared pool. We can set automatic fallback if latency climbs.
[05:34] Aisha: can you quantify the extra memory/cost of running the prefix cache? We need to justify to infra team.
[05:39] Ravi: overhead is roughly cache memory + a small CPU mem for indices. For our sample: a 5M key cache (heavy) is ~6GB; most customers run in the 0.5M - 2M key range initially. We'll show near-term and steady-state numbers in workbook.
[05:52] [06:00] Elena: Quick break — any specific scenario you want us to focus on in the pilot?
[06:03] Markus: payment confirmation + dispute triage. Two flows: high-priority confirmations (low-latency) and async triage (cost-sensitive).
[06:12] Ravi: perfect separation — confirmations benefit from pinned dedicated low-latency pool with smaller model and heavy caching; triage can be batched and run on cheaper instances with higher batching windows.
[06:24] Tom: how do we route between the two?
[06:26] Ravi: Redwood's routing policies let you tag requests or set per-route SLOs. We'll configure route rules: route=confirmation priority=high model=fast-variant pool=dedicated.
[06:36] Markus: show me the math on sample traffic: 500 reqs/min confirmation, average 70 tokens generated per request.
[06:42] Ravi: ok quick calc: 500/min = 30k/hr, at 70 tokens that's 2.1M tokens/hr. If 50% prefix hit then 1.05M tokens saved per hour in compute. Multiply by per-token GPU cost -> big savings. We'll do a full sheet.
[06:58] Aisha: question on replay and audit — if we cache prefixes, where's the audit trail?
[07:03] Elena: audit logs include cache events; we log cache hits/misses at aggregate level and per-request metadata (not full contents) to meet compliance. For Private we can retain logs in your S3 bucket.
[07:15] Markus: ok good. Are there any gotchas with user-level personalization? We don't want to leak PII across templates.
[07:21] Ravi: that's why we recommend prompt normalization and tenant scoping of caches. Also key derivation uses tenant IDs and optional session IDs.
[07:30] Tom: what about TTL eviction patterns — do we risk cold-thrash on release nights when templates change?
[07:36] Ravi: you can do staged rollout: warm caches in advance and TTLs tuned to release cadence. We also support warming APIs.
[07:44] Elena: moving to quantization and model selection briefly — for throughput cost we recommend 4-bit quantized 7B for most flows; bigger models for higher-quality fallback.
[07:55] Markus: do you do auto-quantization or do we need to retrain?
[07:58] Ravi: Redwood supports optimized kernels for quantized models; we usually ship curated quantized variants and recommend validating on your eval set. No retraining required.
[08:06] [08:09] Tom: what about end-to-end latency in Private vs Hosted?
[08:11] Ravi: Private w/ VPC peering can improve network-hop latency slightly but compute is the main factor. Hosted benefits from our global peering in some regions. We'll run benchmarks to measure both.
[08:20] Markus: can we do a quick micro-benchmark today?
[08:23] Ravi: we can demo but data access limits us; better route is we run a 1-hour benchmark in your dev VPC with sample traces. We'll do two runs: baseline and with prefix caching + batching.
[08:34] Aisha: security calibration: we'll need an ATO checklist and details on key rotation.
[08:39] Elena: we'll attach SOC2 artifacts and an ATO checklist.
[08:43] Markus: back to cost numbers — what's the unit cost per generated token you used in your calc?
[08:47] Ravi: in the workbook the baseline we used is $0.0006 per gen token for that model profile; with 50% cache hits and 25% batching efficiency the effective per-token cost becomes ~0.00034 in the example. These are illustrative.
[08:59] Tom: are those numbers including network egress / storage for the cache?
[09:02] Ravi: they include compute + cache storage amortized; network egress minimal for VPC; we can break out the columns.
[09:07] [09:10] Markus: what's the expected ops overhead for running the pilot?
[09:12] Elena: Redwood handles runtime ops; you'll need to provide sample traces and open a peering connection. We'll set a runbook and a single SE touchpoint.
[09:21] Aisha: time estimate for pilot?
[09:23] Ravi: pilot run itself is 1-2 weeks: environment setup (1-3 days), run benchmark and analysis (1-3 days), iterate on TTLs and routing (rest of week).
[09:33] Markus: we have compliance windows — can you support on-call changes?
[09:36] Elena: yes, for Dedicated or Private we can set an on-call rotation as part of the contract; for hosted we have SLA-backed support tiers.
[09:45] Tom: question — how do you handle cold-start for rarely used templates?
[09:49] Ravi: rare templates are expensive; for those we either accept cost or pre-warm on deploys. Another option: route rare templates to smaller models if quality acceptable.
[09:59] Aisha: are there any limitations on the number of cached keys per tenant?
[10:03] Ravi: soft limits by default, adjustable with Dedicated/Private tiers. We'll include recommended caps.
[10:09] Elena: ok let's flip to the workbook shared — key sheets: baseline assumptions, sensitivity analysis, cache sizing, pilot config. Ravi will walk numbers.
[10:18] Ravi: opening sheet — baseline: monthly gen tokens = 30M, average generated tokens per request = 60, peak QPS 250. Column A shows model hourly cost, B shows tokens/sec, C effective per-token. Row for 10/30/50/70% cache hit rate.
[10:36] Markus: in the 50% row what's the monthly cost?
[10:39] Ravi: that example shows ~$4,200/month -> $2,600/month with caching+batching, roughly 38% savings.
[10:46] Tom: what's the sensitivity if hit-rate drops to 20%?
[10:49] Ravi: savings shrink to ~12-18% depending on batching.
[10:53] [11:00] Aisha: ok, on the numbers we want a column that shows break-even time for cache infra cost.
[11:04] Ravi: yes we added a payback calculator — shows you hit payback in 3-6 weeks for mid-range cache sizes at our sample rates.
[11:12] Markus: how do you simulate mix of gen vs embeddings vs rerank? Our workload has both gen & rerank.
[11:18] Ravi: workbook supports multiple route profiles; rerank typically has higher token costs per request but lower QPS; you can split traffic and model mix.
[11:26] Tom: any caveats on function-calling or tool outputs with caching?
[11:30] Ravi: function-calling still benefits from prefix caching for the prompt part; you need to be careful to avoid caching the tool outputs unless deterministic and safe.
[11:39] Markus: can caching introduce stale outputs for dynamic user data?
[11:41] Ravi: if you don't normalize keys it can; hence we advise stripping or injecting user variables outside of cache keys.
[11:48] Aisha: let's talk rollout plan — we want to avoid regressions.
[11:52] Elena: Redwood supports A/B and canary routing; we'll run canary with 5-10% traffic, monitor quality via your eval set and our quality hooks.
[11:59] Markus: what metrics do you recommend to watch?
[12:01] Ravi: p50/p99 latency, cache hit-rate, tokens per request, model quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE or custom evals), error rates and tail latencies.
[12:12] Tom: do you integrate with our observability stack?
[12:14] Elena: yes we can forward traces to Datadog/Lightstep and logs to a customer S3.
[12:19] Aisha: what about cost attribution per product route?
[12:22] Ravi: Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdown per route and per model. We'll show an example dashboard in the deck.
[12:30] Markus: ok, final practical — what do you need from us to get started?
[12:34] Elena: three things: 1) sample traffic trace gzipped with top templates, 2) dev VPC peering connectivity, 3) list of high-priority routes and SLOs.
[12:44] Markus: we can get that by Friday.
[12:47] Tom: what's the pricing model for Dedicated vs Hosted for this optimizer work?
[12:51] Elena: pricing: hosted usage-based; Dedicated has reserved commit + lower per-token unit cost; Private is enterprise license. We'll include price bands in the workbook.
[12:59] Aisha: any competitor wins/losses we should prep for?
[13:02] Elena: customers often compare simple hosted APIs (OpenAI) vs platform features (Redwood). Our differentiation: deeper runtime optimizations, KV/prefix caching and cost attribution.
[13:12] Markus: ok, two quick technical Qs — 1) how is cache persisted across restarts? 2) can we snapshot and restore?
[13:20] Ravi: cache persisted to backing store (configurable: local SSD or S3-backed index); snapshots + restore supported for Private.
[13:28] Tom: do you provide tools to migrate cache keys across model upgrades?
[13:32] Ravi: yes mapping tools and key-versioning. We'll include a runbook.
[13:37] Elena: wrapping up — recap of next steps and action items, then Q&A.
[13:41] Elena: Next steps: we'll send cost-model workbook, SOC2 + network diagram, schedule pilot benchmark. Action items in chat.
[13:49] Markus: sounds good. One more: any recommended defaults for TTL and key hashing?
[13:54] Ravi: defaults we recommend: TTL 12h for templates with daily cadence, 1h for high-velocity templates; key hashing with tenant + template id, strip variable tokens. We'll include param table.
[14:06] Aisha: we'll review the workbook with infra next week.
[14:09] Tom: from product side we'll validate quality with our test prompts.
[14:12] Markus: thanks both, appreciate the detailed walkthrough.
[14:15] Elena: thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the pilot run.
[14:19] (meeting ends)
